questions.q: Two characters argue across a table. Halfway through, the camera crosses to the other side and they suddenly seem to swap places. What has been broken?
questions.explain: Staying on one side of the line between characters keeps screen positions consistent.

questions.q: A film alternates between a bomb ticking under a bus and the hero racing through traffic to reach it. What's the technique?
questions.explain: Cross-cutting alternates simultaneous lines of action, the engine of the last-minute rescue.

questions.q: Which statement about cross-cutting is accurate?
choices: Griffith invented it in The Birth of a Nation
Eisenstein invented it for Battleship Potemkin
It was first used in 2001: A Space Odyssey
Earlier films used it; Griffith developed and popularized it
questions.explain: Pathé's A Narrow Escape (1908) predates Griffith's directing career.

questions.q: Eisenstein cuts three shots of stone lions, sleeping, waking, rising, so a statue seems to roar. What idea of editing does this show?
choices: Shots collide to produce an idea neither contains
Shots are bricks linked in a chain
The camera should follow the actor
questions.explain: Collision, against Pudovkin's linkage and Hollywood's invisibility.

questions.q: An editor has a cut that gets the emotion exactly right but slightly breaks spatial continuity. What would Murch advise?
choices: Keep it: emotion outranks three-dimensional space
questions.explain: In the rule of six, emotion is 51% and 3D space only 4%; sacrifice from the bottom.

questions.q: A character tosses a coin; it spins in the air, and the film cuts to a spinning planet. What's this?
questions.explain: A shared shape and movement join the shots, like the bone and spacecraft in 2001.

questions.q: A feature writer needs to show a team's two years of preparation before a big race, in a few paragraphs. Which film tool is the closest model?
questions.explain: A montage sequence compresses time into quick fragments; use it for change the audience must accept, not feel moment by moment.

ideas: Which approach ranks emotion, story and rhythm above spatial continuity when choosing where to cut?
Which approach insists that two shots should collide to produce an idea neither contains?
Which approach keeps the camera on one side of a line between characters so the audience never loses its bearings?
Which approach alternates between a threatened victim and racing rescuers to build suspense?
